title: Finding the Core
description: How Oldham, Gutenberg, Jeffreys and Lehmann read earthquake waves to find a liquid core and a solid heart

concepts.title: Oldham's Late Arrivals
concepts.contentHtml:
At the end of the nineteenth century most geologists accepted that the Earth was completely solid. Measurements of how the ground rises and falls with the Moon and Sun seemed to back Lord Kelvin's claim that the planet was "as rigid as steel". Then a new kind of evidence arrived. In 1889 Ernst von Rebeur-Paschwitz showed that instruments in Germany had picked up vibrations from an earthquake in Tokyo.1 Waves from a single rupture had crossed the planet's interior, and their timing carried information about everything they had passed through.

The geologist Richard Dixon Oldham made the first decisive use of it. In his 1899 report on the great Assam earthquake of 1897 he gave the first clear evidence for the three main kinds of seismic wave:2 compressional P-waves, shear S-waves and surface waves. Collecting records of later earthquakes, he noticed something odd. At stations on the far side of the Earth, P-waves arrived later than expected.3

Think about what a delay means. A wave that crosses a slow region loses time, and only the deepest paths, those that reach the far side of the planet, cross the centre. Oldham concluded that the Earth has a central core through which P-waves travel much more slowly than through the rock around it. His 1906 paper, "The Constitution of the Interior of the Earth as Revealed by Earthquakes", is usually taken as the discovery of the core.

Read it closely, though. He did not, as is often believed, show that the core is liquid.4 Since everyone assumed a solid Earth, he explained the slowness by a very dense core, probably of iron. Only by 1913, when his records still showed no sign of S-waves crossing the core, did he begin to lean towards a fluid. A correct observation can sit inside an incorrect model for years, and that pattern runs right through the study of the deep Earth.

concepts.title: Gutenberg's Boundary, Jeffreys's Liquid
concepts.contentHtml:
Once seismologists knew the interior had structure, they set out to measure it. Studying earthquake records from 1909, Andrija Mohorovičić found a sharp jump in wave speed at the base of the crust, now called the Moho, about 10 km down under the oceans and up to 50 km under the continents. The core lay far deeper.

Beno Gutenberg, a student of Emil Wiechert at Göttingen, used computational methods developed there to work out how P- and S-wave speeds change with depth. His results showed a major discontinuity at a depth of about 2,900 km: the core–mantle boundary. Modern models put it at 2,891 km, so his figure was remarkably good.1 Yet Gutenberg stayed convinced that the core was solid. He reviewed six methods for estimating its rigidity, and five of them seemed to demand a solid core.2

The decisive argument came from Harold Jeffreys in 1926, and it is a lovely piece of reasoning. Tidal flexing of the solid Earth measures the rigidity of the planet as a whole, while seismic waves measure the rigidity of the mantle. Jeffreys showed that the mantle is much more rigid than the Earth as a whole, so something below the mantle must be far less rigid to bring the average down.3 The only place left was the core, and a core with almost no rigidity is a liquid.

The wave-speed formulas below show why a liquid core casts a shadow. P-waves depend on both the bulk modulus \(K\) and the shear modulus \(\mu\); S-waves depend on \(\mu\) alone. A liquid has \(\mu = 0\), so it cannot carry S-waves at all. S-waves striking the core are stopped, leaving an S-wave shadow on the far side of the planet, while P-waves are bent sharply as they enter the slower liquid, opening a P-wave shadow zone of their own.

concepts.title: Inge Lehmann and P′
concepts.contentHtml:
Inge Lehmann joined the Royal Danish Geodetic Institute in 1925 and headed its seismology department from 1928. She helped build a network of seismograph stations across Denmark and Greenland, and she once recalled that she was "the only Danish seismologist for 25 years". Her stations sat opposite several earthquake hot spots, which gave her an unusual view of waves that had crossed the core.1

Her test case was the 1929 Buller earthquake in New Zealand. If the core were liquid all the way through, stations in the P-wave shadow zone should have recorded nothing strong. Instead two stations squarely inside the shadow recorded unusually large P-wave amplitudes.2 Lehmann gathered travel times and amplitudes from stations across Europe and worked through them by hand. Her cousin Nils Groes remembered her one summer Sunday in her garden, at a table covered in oatmeal boxes full of cardboard cards, each card holding an earthquake and its arrival times around the world.

Her 1936 paper had one of the shortest titles in science: P′, the notation for P-waves that pass through the mantle into the core and back out again. She proposed a three-shell Earth: a solid mantle, a liquid outer core and an inner core in which waves travel faster, refracting energy into the shadow zone. She put its boundary at a radius of about 1,400 km.3 Fellow seismologists were quickly won over, and in the following years others, Jeffreys among them, added evidence for it.

Notice what she did and did not show. A faster inner region explains the arrivals, but it says nothing directly about whether that region is solid. Solidity was not conclusively established until the early 1970s,4 when measurements of the Earth's free oscillations, the slow ringing of the whole planet after great earthquakes, settled it. Lehmann lived to be 104, long enough to see it.

title: Seismic Tomography
description: How millions of seismograms become 3D maps of the mantle, from sinking slabs to the limits of resolution

concepts.title: From One Dimension to Three
concepts.contentHtml:
To first order the Earth is an onion: its properties depend mainly on depth. From the Moho to the core–mantle boundary, density and both P- and S-wave speeds rise by about 70%.1 Seismologists capture this in one-dimensional reference models, the best known being the Preliminary Reference Earth Model (PREM) of Adam Dziewoński and Don Anderson, published in 1981. PREM was built from the travel times of seismic phases, the frequencies of the Earth's free oscillations and astrometric data.2

Seismic tomography maps the departures from that onion. Every recorded wave has a predicted arrival time in the reference model; the difference, the travel-time residual, adds up the small speed anomalies along the wave's path, as the formula below shows. One residual cannot tell you where along the path the anomaly lies. Millions of paths crossing at different angles can, in the way a medical CT scanner rebuilds a body from X-rays sent through it from many directions. The first global maps, by Dziewoński and colleagues in 1977 and by John Woodhouse and Dziewoński in 1984, made clear that plate tectonics is intimately linked to processes deep inside the planet.3

The anomalies are small. Away from the top and bottom of the mantle, lateral variations in wave speed and density do not exceed a few per cent.4 A slow region might be hotter than its surroundings, chemically different or partly molten, and tomography alone often cannot say which. Steady progress over the following decades owes most to networks of broadband seismometers, openly shared data and computing power that lets seismologists use millions of seismograms. Modern full-waveform methods go further still, fitting whole stretches of each seismogram with numerical simulations, such as the spectral element method, rather than using first arrival times alone.

concepts.title: Slabs All the Way Down
concepts.contentHtml:
For decades a quarrel ran through the Earth sciences. Some researchers argued for a layered mantle, convecting separately above and below about 660 km and so keeping chemically distinct reservoirs apart. Others favoured whole-mantle convection. Tomography offered a direct test: follow the cold, fast slabs of sinking ocean floor and see where they go.

In 1997 Rob van der Hilst, Sri Widiyantoro and E. R. Engdahl published P-wave images built from improved earthquake locations. They resolved long, narrow, fast structures in the lower mantle, some of which could be followed up to today's subduction zones, and they concluded that at least some slab segments seem to sink to the bottom of the mantle.1 That was strong evidence for mantle-wide flow.

The fuller picture is messier and more interesting. Some slabs appear to lie flat above the 660 km boundary, as beneath Izu-Bonin and Honshu, while others, such as the Marianas and Aegean slabs, have crossed it.2 In 2013 Fukao and Obayashi argued for a third group, including Java, Kermadec and Peru, that stalls above about 1,000 km depth.3 The resistance at 660 km has two parts: the phase change there absorbs heat (it is endothermic, as the next lesson explains), and viscosity rises by one or two orders of magnitude.

Deeper still lies a slab graveyard. At 1,500 and 2,800 km depth, fast structures mark the remains of the Tethys, Farallon and Mongol-Okhotsk slabs, oceanic plates that subducted in the Permian and the Mesozoic.4 Beneath the Americas, an elongated fast anomaly reaching about 1,500 km depth is linked to the Farallon Plate, which subducted beneath North America. Tomography has become a kind of plate-tectonic archaeology: you can read the history of vanished oceans from the cold rock they left behind.

concepts.title: How Far to Trust a Tomogram
concepts.contentHtml:
A tomographic model is the answer to an inverse problem with far more unknowns than clean constraints, and you should read it like one. Earthquakes cluster along plate boundaries and most seismometers sit on land, so some regions are crossed by thousands of rays and others by almost none. To get a stable answer, modellers add regularisation: preferences for smooth models with modest anomalies. Those choices strongly affect how large the recovered anomalies come out, and different groups make them differently.1

Geometry adds bias. Waves from distant earthquakes travel nearly vertically through the upper mantle, so travel-time models struggle to say at what depth an anomaly sits in the top 700–1,000 km. Seismologists check resolution with synthetic tests. In a checkerboard test you invent a pattern of alternating fast and slow cells, compute the data it would produce with the real ray coverage, invert those data and see what survives. Such tests can mislead, because a checkerboard represents only a single wavelength of heterogeneity.2

Some structures are almost invisible. A narrow, purely thermal plume barely disturbs a passing wave,3 and diffraction lets the wavefront heal on its way to the surface. Calculations suggest delays from thermal plumes in the lower mantle of less than a second,4 so a thin plume tail can be missed entirely, or smeared into something broader than it is.

So what can you trust? Features that many independently built models agree on. In a 2020 review, Jeroen Ritsema and Vedran Lekić sorted velocity profiles from many models by cluster analysis and found strong agreement on the largest structures, above all two antipodal slow regions at the base of the mantle, which you meet in lesson 4. The next generation of models will draw on ocean-bottom seismometers, autonomous hydrophones and fibre-optic cables used as dense seismic arrays.

title: The Transition Zone and Its Hidden Water
description: The 410 and 660 km phase changes, ringwoodite in a diamond and the debate over deep water

concepts.title: Two Steps in the Mantle: 410 and 660
concepts.contentHtml:
Between about 410 and 660 km depth lies the mantle transition zone, bounded by two sharp jumps in seismic wave speed. They are not changes of rock type but changes of crystal structure. The upper mantle is dominated by olivine, (Mg,Fe)₂SiO₄, and as pressure rises its atoms repack into denser arrangements. Near 410 km olivine becomes wadsleyite; near 520 km wadsleyite becomes ringwoodite; and near 660 km ringwoodite breaks down into two lower-mantle minerals,1 bridgmanite (once called silicate perovskite) and ferropericlase.

The depth of each transition depends on temperature, and the slope of that dependence, the Clapeyron slope, has opposite signs at the two boundaries. The 410 transition is exothermic with a positive slope, so in a cold sinking slab it happens at lower pressure and the boundary bulges upward. The 660 transition is endothermic with a negative slope, estimated at −0.4 to −2.0 MPa/K, so in a cold slab it is pushed tens of kilometres deeper.2 That matters mechanically. Inside the slab the rock stays in the lighter ringwoodite form while the mantle around it has already turned denser, so the slab gains buoyancy that resists its descent.

This makes the two boundaries a thermometer. Mapping their depths with waves that reflect off them or convert at them shows that their topography mainly reflects mantle temperature, and so present-day flow. Their behaviour is largely consistent with an olivine-rich mantle at a potential temperature of about 1,600 K.3 Yet in many places the 410 and the 660 do not move together, a sign that the transition zone holds up the passage of cold material from above and hot material from below.4

concepts.title: A Diamond from Juína
concepts.contentHtml:
Nobody can drill into the transition zone, so for decades its minerals were known only from laboratory experiments. Those experiments raised a striking possibility. Wadsleyite and ringwoodite, unlike olivine, can hold water in their crystal structure, not as liquid but as hydroxyl bound into the lattice, up to around 2.5% of their weight.1 If the transition zone were even partly saturated, it could be one of the planet's largest water reservoirs. Whether it actually holds much water was hotly contested, and electrical-conductivity studies gave conflicting answers.

In 2014 Graham Pearson and colleagues reported evidence from an unlikely messenger, a diamond from Juína, Brazil. Using X-ray diffraction, Raman and infrared spectroscopy, they identified an inclusion of ringwoodite: the first higher-pressure form of olivine ever found in a rock from Earth.2 The diamond had served as a pressure capsule, carrying the mineral up from the transition zone without letting it revert to olivine. Infrared absorption showed the inclusion was water-rich, direct evidence that, at least locally, the transition zone is hydrous, to about 1% by weight.3 The find also showed that some kimberlites, the volcanic rocks that carry diamonds to the surface, have their roots this deep.

More messengers followed. In 2018 Oliver Tschauner's team reported ice-VII, a high-pressure form of water ice, trapped in diamonds, pointing to fluid-rich pockets in the upper transition zone and around 660 km.4 In 2022 a gem diamond from the Karowe mine in Botswana held ringwoodite with ferropericlase and enstatite, fixing its origin at about 23.5 GPa and 1,650 °C, right at the 660 km boundary, in a water-saturated setting.5

Keep the caveat in view. Each diamond samples one tiny spot, and as the geophysicist Steve Jacobsen put it, whether such a unique sample is representative of the Earth's interior is not known.6

concepts.title: An Ocean's Worth of Water?
concepts.contentHtml:
A single diamond cannot tell you how much water the whole transition zone holds, so Brandon Schmandt and Steve Jacobsen looked for a regional signature. Their idea was dehydration melting. Ringwoodite can hold a lot of water, but the bridgmanite that forms below 660 km can hold almost none.1 If water-rich rock is carried down across the boundary, the water has to go somewhere, and a little of the rock melts.

They tested the idea in two ways. In the laboratory, Jacobsen squeezed water-bearing ringwoodite between diamond anvils to the conditions near 660 km; as it transformed into bridgmanite and (Mg,Fe)O, melt appeared between the grains. In the field, Schmandt used USArray, a dense network of more than 2,000 seismometers across the United States,2 to look for P-waves converting to S-waves at sharp drops in velocity. They found abrupt decreases in seismic speed just below 660 km where mantle appears to be flowing down, consistent with partial melt.3 Their 2014 paper in Science concluded that a large region of the transition zone beneath North America is hydrated, and that dehydration melting may act to trap water there, like a filter at the bottom of a sink.

The headline numbers need care. If just 1% of the transition zone's weight were water, the researchers said, that would be equivalent to nearly three times the water in the oceans.4 But 1% is the value from one diamond, and evidence from around the globe points to variable hydration, with some partial melting near the top of the transition zone too.5 Whether the deep mantle holds a fraction of an ocean or several is still debated, and the answer matters: it governs how much of the surface ocean has cycled through the interior by subduction over Earth's history, and how much might still be stored there.

title: Continents at the Bottom of the Mantle
description: D″, post-perovskite, the two LLSVPs, ultra-low velocity zones and where they came from, Theia included

concepts.title: D″ and the Two Great Provinces
concepts.contentHtml:
The lowest few hundred kilometres of the mantle, just above the core, are known as D″ ("D double-prime"). The mantle here is heated from below by the core and fed from above by sinking slabs. In 2004 Motohiko Murakami, Kei Hirose and colleagues squeezed and heated MgSiO₃ to core–mantle boundary conditions and watched with X-ray diffraction as bridgmanite turned into a new structure of stacked sheets above 125 GPa and 2,500 K, the conditions about 2,700 km down.1 This post-perovskite phase is 1.0–1.2% denser, and its transition may explain the D″ discontinuity and the strong seismic anisotropy below it.2

Seen at the scale of the whole planet, D″ is dominated by something bigger. Since the 1980s tomography has shown two enormous regions of slow shear-wave speed, one beneath Africa and one beneath the Pacific, on almost exactly opposite sides of the Earth. Once called superplumes, they are now the large low-shear-velocity provinces (LLSVPs). They are thousands of kilometres across and rise about 1,000 km above the core.3 Spread over the surface, their material would make a layer about 100 km thick around the entire planet.4 Kevin Burke, Trond Torsvik and Pavel Doubrovine dubbed them5 Tuzo (The Unmoved Zone Of the Earth's deep mantle, under Africa) and Jason (Just As Stable ON the opposite meridian, under the Pacific), acronyms that spell the names of two hotspot pioneers you meet in the next lesson.

Their edges are a clue. Along the margins of the LLSVPs, shear-wave speed changes by several per cent over less than 100 km.6 Heat diffuses and tends to blur boundaries, so a sharp wall hints at a change in composition, although some simulations show that a strongly temperature-dependent viscosity can sharpen purely thermal edges too.

concepts.title: Ultra-Low Velocity Zones
concepts.contentHtml:
Zoom in on the core–mantle boundary and the strangest structures appear. Ultra-low velocity zones (ULVZs) are thin patches sitting right on the core, typically up to hundreds of kilometres wide but only tens of kilometres thick, in which S-wave speeds drop by up to 30% and P-wave speeds by up to 10%.1 Seismologists began mapping them in the 1990s, and seismic models fit them best with density increases of up to 10%.2 For comparison, the LLSVPs above them are slow by only a few per cent.

They are hard to see. A favourite probe is SPdKS, a wave that goes down as S, runs briefly along the core–mantle boundary as a diffracted P-wave, crosses the core and climbs back as S. A ULVZ in its path distorts the waveform. A 2020 study by Michael Thorne and colleagues combed 58,155 such recordings, which together sample 56.9% of the boundary's area, and identified sixteen new candidate regions.3 Much of the boundary is still poorly surveyed.

Where they have been found, ULVZs are concentrated beneath and along the margins of the LLSVPs,4 and a few are huge: mega-ULVZs extending up to 1,000 km across. Large ULVZs are known beneath Hawaii, Iceland and Samoa. In 2017 Kaiqing Yuan and Barbara Romanowicz used shear waves diffracted along the core to illuminate the root of the Iceland plume from several directions, and found a large ULVZ that is close to axisymmetric.

What are they? There are two main families of explanation. They may be partial melt, the hottest rock at the bottom of the mantle beginning to melt, which fits the huge drop in S-wave speed because a liquid has no rigidity. Or they may be compositionally distinct, for example extremely iron-rich ferropericlase, which is dense and seismically slow; combinations of both are possible.5 Yuan and Romanowicz favoured partial melting of a locally thickened, denser and hotter layer at the plume root.6

concepts.title: Hot, Heavy or Alien?
concepts.contentHtml:
Are the LLSVPs simply hot, or are they made of different stuff? In purely thermal models they are clusters of hot upwellings that tomography blurs into broad blobs. In thermochemical models they are dense piles, shaped and shoved around by the slabs sinking beside them, which would explain their sharp edges and long-term stability.

The cleanest test is density, and two clever methods disagree. In 2017 Harriet Lau and colleagues used GPS measurements of the body tide, the twice-daily flexing of the solid Earth under the Moon and Sun, and found the bottom two-thirds of the LLSVPs about 0.5% denser than average mantle.1 The same year Paula Koelemeijer, Arwen Deuss and Jeroen Ritsema used Stoneley modes, free oscillations concentrated at the core–mantle boundary, and found the provinces less dense overall, though they could not rule out a dense layer about 100 km thick at the base.2 One proposed reconciliation is that only the lowest 100 km or so is anomalously dense.3

If the piles are chemically distinct, where did they come from? Three families of answer compete:

  • Recycled crust: basaltic ocean crust becomes denser than ordinary mantle at lower-mantle pressures, so it may peel off slabs and pile up over billions of years.4
  • Primordial material: dense leftovers of the Earth's earliest differentiation, such as the remains of a basal magma ocean that crystallised at the bottom of the mantle.
  • Theia: in 2023 Qian Yuan and colleagues proposed that the provinces are buried relics of Theia's mantle, preserved after the giant impact that formed the Moon.5 Because the Moon is rich in iron oxide, they estimated Theia's mantle to be 2.0–3.5% denser than Earth's,6 dense enough to sink, gather into piles and survive 4.5 billion years of convection.7

The Theia idea is elegant but untested, and the older explanations remain very much alive. One test could come from plume lavas, if they turn out to carry a chemical fingerprint that only Theia could have left.

title: The Mantle Plume Debate
description: Wilson's hotspots, Morgan's plumes, the first images of deep conduits and the sceptics' shallow alternative

concepts.title: Wilson's Hotspots, Morgan's Plumes
concepts.contentHtml:
Hawaii is an awkward fact for plate tectonics. Its volcanoes rise in the middle of the Pacific Plate, more than 3,200 km from the nearest plate boundary.1 In 1963 the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson proposed that the Hawaiian Island–Emperor Seamounts chain formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a deep, stationary hotspot. Magma erupts on the sea floor as a seamount, which grows until it emerges as an island volcano; plate motion then carries it off the hotspot, its volcanism ceases, and a new volcano grows over the hotspot behind it. The prediction is an age progression, and it holds: the oldest rocks on Kauai are about 5.5 million years old and deeply eroded, while the Big Island's oldest exposed rocks are less than 0.7 million years old.2

In 1971 W. Jason Morgan gave the hotspot a deep source in a Nature paper titled "Convection Plumes in the Lower Mantle". He showed that the Hawaiian–Emperor, Tuamotu–Line and Austral–Gilbert–Marshall chains could all be generated by a rigid Pacific Plate rotating over three fixed hotspots,3 and he proposed that hotspots are fed by columns of hot rock rising from the deep mantle: mantle plumes.

The plume hypothesis makes testable claims, which is what makes it good science:

  • Deep roots: plumes begin as instabilities in a hot thermal boundary layer, at the core–mantle boundary or at the edges of the LLSVPs.4
  • Fixity: plumes move slowly relative to one another, so hotspots form a nearly fixed frame against which plates move.
  • Heat and chemistry: plume rock should be hotter than ordinary mantle and may carry distinctive deep material into ocean-island lavas.
  • Tracks: volcanoes should age steadily along each chain.

More than a hundred hotspots have been active in the past 10 million years,5 from Iceland and the Galápagos to Yellowstone. Whether all of them, or only some, fit these predictions is the heart of the debate.

concepts.title: Seeing Plumes
concepts.contentHtml:
If plumes exist, why are they so hard to see? Geodynamic models predict that a purely thermal plume has a tail only several hundred kilometres wide, and, as lesson 2 showed, thin tails heal out of seismic wavefronts. Imaging them took new methods.

In 2004 Raffaella Montelli, Guust Nolet and colleagues used finite-frequency tomography, which treats a seismic wave as sensitive to a broad region around its ray rather than to a thin line. Their P-wave images showed at least six well-resolved plumes reaching the lowermost mantle, beneath Ascension, the Azores, the Canaries, Easter Island, Samoa and Tahiti,1 while several other plumes seemed confined to the upper mantle. The study was controversial at the time, but later independent work also resolved whole-mantle, plume-like structures.2

In 2015 Scott French and Barbara Romanowicz went further with full-waveform tomography, computing the complete wavefield numerically and fitting whole seismograms. They found broad, nearly vertical conduits beneath many prominent hotspots, extending from the core–mantle boundary to about 1,000 km below the surface, where some bend sideways as if caught in faster upper-mantle flow.3 At the base, the conduits beneath Hawaii, Iceland and Samoa are rooted in known large ULVZs. The conduits are broader than classic thermal plume tails, which suggests they are long-lived and perhaps thermochemical, and their verticality implies very sluggish flow below 1,000 km.

A second line of evidence comes from history. Trond Torsvik, Kevin Burke and colleagues rotated large igneous provinces and kimberlites back to where they erupted. More than 90% of the reconstructed sites lay above the edges of Tuzo and Jason,4 suggesting that plumes rise from plume generation zones at the margins of the LLSVPs, and that the provinces have stayed put for about 0.55 billion years. Whether that correlation is real, and whether the LLSVPs can stay fixed so long, is still debated.5

concepts.title: The Sceptics' Case
concepts.contentHtml:
Not everyone accepts that hotspots need deep plumes. The best-developed alternative is the Plate model, championed by Gillian Foulger of Durham University. It attributes melting anomalies to shallow processes tied to plate tectonics: volcanism occurs where the lithosphere is being stretched,1 and the volume of melt depends mainly on how fertile, that is how easily melted, the underlying mantle is. Supporters point out that most present-day hotspots erupt on or near spreading ridges or in rifts and other regions that are extending,2 and that hotspots vary so much that a "one size fits all" plume model looks inappropriate.

The fixity claim has also taken a hit. The sharp bend in the Hawaiian–Emperor chain was long read as a change in the Pacific Plate's direction over a stationary hotspot. Ocean Drilling Program Leg 197 tested this by drilling the Emperor Seamounts and measuring, from the magnetism frozen into their lavas, the latitude at which each had formed. The latitudes changed with age: the Emperor chain formed mainly while the Hawaiian hotspot itself moved south at a rapid 4–5 cm per year, between about 81 and 47 million years ago.3 The bend may record a drifting plume in a convecting mantle as much as a turning plate.4 Even the authors of the US Geological Survey's classic booklet This Dynamic Earth later added a note that new studies suggest hotspots are neither deep nor fixed.5

Where does that leave you? Neither side has won outright. A moving plume is still a plume, and tomography now shows deep conduits beneath Hawaii, Iceland, Samoa and others. But the same studies find some plumes confined to the upper mantle, and limited resolution makes the conditions beneath many hotspots hard to pin down. A reasonable reading of the evidence is that some hotspots are fed by deep plumes and others probably are not.

title: The Geodynamo and the Age of the Inner Core
description: How the core makes the field, why conductivity matters and what ancient rocks say about the inner core's birth

concepts.title: A Self-Sustaining Dynamo
concepts.contentHtml:
A bar magnet cannot explain the Earth's field: iron loses its magnetism at the temperatures of the core.1 In 1946 Walter Elsasser proposed instead that the field is made by a dynamo. Liquid iron in the outer core conducts electricity; as it flows across an existing magnetic field it induces electric currents, and those currents generate magnetic field of their own. If the flow is vigorous and organised enough, the field it regenerates can sustain itself indefinitely, with no permanent magnet anywhere.

The balance is set by the induction equation, shown below. The first term on the right stretches and twists field lines with the flow \(\mathbf{u}\); the second lets the field decay through electrical resistance, at a rate set by the magnetic diffusivity \(\eta\). Their ratio is the magnetic Reynolds number, and a dynamo works only when stretching beats decay.

Something must keep the iron moving. The core has three power sources: heat released as the core cools, latent heat released as the solid inner core freezes, and compositional convection.2 When iron freezes onto the inner core it rejects lighter elements such as oxygen, sulphur or silicon, and the buoyant, enriched liquid rises from the bottom of the outer core. That makes the inner core a crucial part of the engine: once it exists, it stirs the outer core from below.

For a long time no one could show that such a dynamo actually works in three dimensions. In 1995 Gary Glatzmaier and Paul Roberts published a self-consistent computer simulation that maintained a magnetic field for over 40,000 simulated years.3 Their model, which included an electrically conducting inner core, went through several polarity excursions and then, near the end of the run, a complete reversal of the dipole.4 The simulated reversal shared some features with real ones, and dynamo models are now a central tool for asking what the field looked like before the inner core existed.

concepts.title: The Conductivity Crisis
concepts.contentHtml:
The core's power budget hinges on one awkward number: the thermal conductivity of iron alloy at core conditions. Heat conducted out along the adiabat, the temperature profile of a well-mixed fluid, leaks away without driving any flow. Only the heat flow beyond that conducted amount can power thermal convection, so the higher the conductivity, the less is left for the dynamo.

In 2012 Monica Pozzo, Chris Davies, David Gubbins and Dario Alfè calculated the conductivities of liquid iron mixtures from first principles, using density functional theory. They came out two to three times higher than the values then in use.1 The adiabatic heat flux at the core–mantle boundary rose to 15–16 terawatts, more than the mantle was thought to extract.2 The top of the core would be thermally stratified, much of the dynamo would have to run on compositional convection, and the inner core would have to be young. Paul Olson called the result the new core paradox: a young inner core and a hot early core, yet a magnetic field recorded in very ancient rocks.

Experiments split. In 2016 Kenji Ohta and colleagues measured the electrical resistivity of iron at up to 4,500 K and megabar pressures in a laser-heated diamond-anvil cell; the low resistivity implied high thermal conductivity, rapid core cooling and an inner core less than 0.7 billion years old.3 The same year Zuzana Konôpková and colleagues measured the thermal conductivity of solid iron directly and found 18–44 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, near the low end of previous estimates, which allows an inner core as old as the dynamo itself.4

A second puzzle sharpens the first. Liquids must be supercooled before crystals form spontaneously, and classical nucleation theory says the core needed several hundred kelvin of supercooling, incompatible with its present-day temperature.5 This inner-core nucleation paradox implies the inner core should not exist. A 2025 molecular dynamics study by Alfred Wilson and colleagues found that iron with 10–15% carbon is compatible with a range of geophysical constraints.6

concepts.title: Dating the Inner Core from Rocks
concepts.contentHtml:
If theory cannot settle the inner core's age, perhaps the rocks can. When the inner core began to freeze, the outer core should have switched to a new convective regime, driven from below by compositional buoyancy, and the field it produced should have changed. Palaeointensity studies measure the strength of ancient fields from the magnetism locked into rocks and crystals as they cooled, so in principle you can look for the inner core's birthday in the record.

The candidates span an enormous range. Thermal models with different plausible conductivities put the onset of inner-core growth anywhere from about 0.5 to more than 2.5 billion years ago.1 Two palaeomagnetic studies point to very different answers:

  • In 2015 Andrew Biggin and colleagues screened an expanded database of Precambrian intensities with new reliability criteria and found a clear rise in both average field strength and variability between 1 and 1.5 billion years ago,2 which they read as inner-core nucleation and a sign of modest conductivity.
  • In 2019 Richard Bono, John Tarduno and colleagues measured single crystals of plagioclase and clinopyroxene from the roughly 565-million-year-old Sept-Îles intrusive suite. The Ediacaran field was the weakest yet reported from such rocks, more than ten times weaker than today's,3 with widely scattered directions and signs of very frequent reversals. They read it as a faltering dynamo just before the inner core began to grow.

At the other end of history lies the question of when the dynamo started at all. In 2015 Tarduno's group reported fields recorded in zircon crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia aged 3.3 to 4.2 billion years.4 In 2020 Cauê Borlina, Benjamin Weiss and colleagues countered that most of these zircons are poor recorders whose magnetisation was acquired later, leaving the dynamo before 3.5 billion years ago unknown.5 Tarduno's group replied with new analyses supporting a primary record.6 The stakes are high, because a strong early field with no inner core needs some other power source, such as chemical precipitation out of the cooling liquid core.

title: The Restless Inner Core
description: Anisotropy, an innermost inner core and the contested evidence that the inner core speeds up and backtracks

concepts.title: A Textured Heart
concepts.contentHtml:
The inner core is not a uniform ball. In 1986 seismologists found that it is anisotropic: P-waves crossing it parallel to the Earth's spin axis travel faster than waves crossing it in the equatorial plane, where the slowest direction lies. The usual explanation is that the inner core's iron crystals are partly aligned, perhaps by the way it grew or has deformed, though how the alignment arose is still argued over.

In 2002 Miaki Ishii and Adam Dziewoński proposed something deeper: an innermost inner core about 300 km in radius, with its own distinct anisotropy.1 Inside it, the slowest direction is about 45° from east–west rather than east–west itself. It was the first new spherical shell proposed in the Earth since Lehmann's discovery in 1936,2 and they suggested it might be a fossil of an early phase in the inner core's history.

The trouble is that very few rays sample the centre of the Earth. You need an earthquake and a seismometer almost exactly opposite each other, yet large earthquakes cluster in a belt near the equator and stations are scarce in the oceans.3 In 2023 Thanh-Son Phạm and Hrvoje Tkalčić found a way round it. By stacking waveforms from many stations for single large earthquakes, such as the magnitude 7.9 Solomon Islands earthquake of 22 January 2017, they detected waves that bounced along the Earth's diameter up to five times, crossing the inner core again and again.4

Those reverberations favour a distinct innermost ball with a radius of about 650 km, in which P-waves are about 4% slower at roughly 50° to the rotation axis, surrounded by a weakly anisotropic outer shell.5 The two studies agree that the centre is different but not on its size, a reminder of how thin the data are. Phạm and Tkalčić suggest the innermost ball could be a fossilised record of a significant global event in the Earth's past.

concepts.title: Does the Inner Core Spin Faster?
concepts.contentHtml:
The inner core is a solid ball floating in liquid iron, tugged magnetically by the flowing outer core and gravitationally by dense regions of the mantle. Nothing forces it to turn at exactly the rate of the rest of the planet, so measuring its rotation tests how the Earth's layers are coupled.

The method relies on earthquake doublets: pairs of earthquakes in almost the same place, years apart, whose waves follow almost the same path to the same stations. If nothing has changed, the seismograms match; if the inner core has turned, the waves sample a slightly different part of it and the records differ. In 1996 Xiaodong Song and Paul Richards found a small, systematic change over three decades in the travel times of waves crossing the inner core, best explained by rotation carrying its anisotropy with it, about 1° per year faster than the mantle.1 Later estimates shrank dramatically, settling at about 0.05–0.15° per year.2

In 2023 Yi Yang and Song compared repeating South Sandwich Islands earthquakes recorded in Alaska back to 1964. Paths that had changed in earlier decades had barely changed over the past ten years, suggesting the differential rotation had recently paused3 and was turning back, as part of an oscillation of roughly seven decades with an earlier turning point in the early 1970s.4 They noted that this period matches changes in the length of day and the magnetic field.

Not everyone agrees on the clock. In 2022 Wei Wang and John Vidale used pairs of precisely located nuclear tests and found the inner core sub-rotated at least 0.1° from 1969 to 1971, then super-rotated about 0.29° from 1971 to 1974,5 which they fitted with a six-year oscillation that also matches a six-year rhythm in the length of day. And in 2006 Lianxing Wen argued that some changes come from the inner core's surface rather than its spin: he found waves reflected off the inner core arriving 39–70 milliseconds earlier in 2003 than in 1993, as if the core had grown locally by about 1–2 km beneath middle Africa.6

concepts.title: Backtracking, and a Changing Surface
concepts.contentHtml:
The clearest test so far came in 2024. Wei Wang, John Vidale and colleagues assembled 143 pairs of repeating earthquakes, built from 121 South Sandwich Islands earthquakes between 1991 and 2023,1 and examined their inner-core waves (PKIKP) at two arrays in northern North America, at Eielson in Alaska and Yellowknife in Canada. They found waveform reversals: records that changed and then, years later, changed back to match earlier events. A match means the inner core has returned to a position, relative to the mantle, that it occupied before.

Chaining these matches together, they concluded that the inner core super-rotated gradually from 2003 to 2008 and then, from 2008 to 2023, sub-rotated back along the same path two to three times more slowly.2 Be clear about what that means. The inner core never stopped spinning; it turns with the Earth once a day, and the measurements track only its tiny lead or lag relative to the mantle. The difference between the forward and backward rates, they wrote, means new models will be needed for how the inner core, outer core and mantle interact.

In 2025 Vidale's group extended the data and found a twist. Between 2004 and 2008 some changes appeared at Yellowknife but not at Eielson,3 even at times when the inner core had returned to the same position. Yellowknife's rays only graze the top of the inner core, while Eielson's dive deeper, so the extra changes point to the shallow inner core itself changing. Their verdict on the long-running dispute between rotation and local surface change was that the answer is tentatively both.4 The likely cause is viscous deformation of the inner-core boundary, driven by gravitational coupling with dense regions of the mantle or by drag from convection in the outer core.5

Open questions remain at every timescale: whether the main rhythm is six years or seventy, why forward and backward motion differ, and how much the inner core's slow wanderings contribute to tiny changes in the length of your day.
